text:
For many Nigerian business owners, the struggle to keep their businesses alive has gone beyond the usual challenges of high operating costs, poor electricity supply, rising fuel prices and limited access to loans. In many parts of the country, staying in business has also become a battle against insecurity.
A farmer who is afraid to visit his farmland, a trader who must close his shop before sunset, a transporter who avoids certain roads because of kidnapping and a manufacturer who struggles to move goods safely all have one thing in common: insecurity has become part of their daily business challenges.
Over the last five years, from 2021 to 2026, Nigeria has continued to face different forms of insecurity, including banditry, kidnapping, terrorism, farmer-herder violence, armed robbery and attacks on communities. Although these incidents have different causes and occur in different parts of the country, their effects have spread beyond the communities directly affected.
Businesses have lost customers, farmers have abandoned their land, traders have reduced their activities, transporters have increased fares and investors have become more careful about where they put their money.
The consequences are not limited to those who have lost their lives, properties or loved ones. They are also reflected in the prices of food, transportation, goods and services that ordinary Nigerians pay for every day.
What makes the situation more worrying is that many businesses were already struggling with economic difficulties. The removal of fuel subsidies, the depreciation of the naira, inflation and high electricity costs have placed serious pressure on business owners. Insecurity has added another burden, making it harder for many businesses to survive.
Farmers: When going to the farm becomes a risk Agriculture is one of the sectors that has suffered heavily from Nigeria’s security challenges.
For millions of Nigerians, farming is not just a source of food but also a major source of income. Farmers cultivate rice, maize, yam, cassava, beans and other crops that supply markets across the country.
However, in several farming communities, the fear of attacks and kidnapping has changed the way people work.
In parts of Kaduna, Katsina, Zamfara, Niger, Benue and Plateau states, farmers have faced attacks, threats, killings and abductions. Some have been forced to leave their communities, while others have abandoned their farmlands because they are afraid of being attacked while working.
For a farmer who depends on the rainy season to plant crops, missing the planting period can mean losing an entire year’s income.
Some farmers have also had to pay money to armed groups before they can access their farms. Others have been forced to sell their properties or borrow money to pay ransom after family members were kidnapped.
A Reuters report published in June 2024 documented how attacks in Katsina forced farmers to abandon their farms after gunmen killed residents, abducted others and destroyed crops. The report also highlighted how armed groups demanded payments from communities before allowing farming activities to continue.
The effect of this situation goes beyond individual farmers. When farmers cannot cultivate their land, the quantity of food available for sale reduces. When supply becomes limited, prices can increase, putting pressure on households and businesses that depend on agricultural produce.
The United States Department of Commerce’s 2025 report on Nigeria’s agricultural sector identified insecurity, rising input costs, climate change and poor transportation as some of the challenges limiting agricultural production.
This means that while farmers are expected to produce more food to meet the needs of a growing population, some are struggling to protect themselves, their families and their investments.
The situation has also affected agricultural workers, food processors, wholesalers and retailers who depend on farmers for regular supplies.
For example, a food-processing company that depends on maize or cassava cannot operate efficiently when its suppliers are unable to deliver enough raw materials. A trader who buys tomatoes, onions or grains from northern markets may also face supply difficulties when insecurity disrupts movement.
In the end, the impact is felt by consumers who have to pay more for food.
Traders and market owners count their losses Markets are important to Nigeria’s economy because they provide income for millions of people and connect producers with consumers. But in areas affected by insecurity, market activities have been disrupted by fear, attacks and restrictions on movement.
In some communities, traders have reduced their business hours because they are afraid of travelling early in the morning or returning home late at night. Others have moved their businesses to safer locations, while some have completely shut down.
For traders who depend on customers from surrounding villages, insecurity can mean losing a large part of their market.
A market that once attracted hundreds of buyers and sellers can become quiet when residents flee their communities or refuse to travel because of safety concerns.
The situation is particularly difficult for small business owners who depend on daily sales to survive.
A woman selling foodstuff, a provision store owner, a clothes seller or a local restaurant operator may not have enough savings to survive several days without customers.
Unlike large companies, many small businesses cannot afford private security, insurance or alternative business locations.
When business activities stop, workers may lose their jobs, suppliers lose customers and families lose their daily income. This creates a chain of economic difficulties that can affect an entire community.
Transportation and logistics: The additional cost of moving goods Transportation is another area where insecurity has affected business activities across Nigeria.
Goods must move from farms to markets, from warehouses to shops and from manufacturers to consumers. However, insecurity along some major highways and rural roads has made transportation more difficult and expensive.
Kidnapping and attacks on travellers have created fear among drivers, passengers and transport companies. Some drivers avoid certain routes, while others travel in groups or during daylight hours to reduce their exposure to danger.
For transporters who continue to operate on risky routes, the fear of attacks can increase operating costs. They may spend more on security arrangements, change their routes or charge higher fares to cover additional expenses.
Longer routes also mean more fuel consumption, longer delivery times and higher maintenance costs. These additional expenses are eventually transferred to business owners and consumers.
For example, a trader who buys goods from another state may have to spend more on transportation before bringing those goods to the market. To avoid making a loss, the trader may increase selling prices.
Manufacturers also face difficulties when raw materials and finished products cannot reach their destinations on time. For businesses that operate with limited profit margins, delays and additional transportation costs can reduce their earnings.
The problem is not limited to northern Nigeria. Businesses across the country depend on an effective road network to move goods and people. When insecurity makes some routes unsafe, the entire supply chain can suffer.
Small businesses: The struggle to survive Small and medium-sized enterprises are among the businesses most exposed to the effects of insecurity. These businesses include shops, restaurants, filling stations, supermarkets, transport operators, workshops, farms, hotels and other service providers.
Many of them operate with limited capital and depend on daily sales to pay workers, suppliers, rent and other expenses. When insecurity affects their location, customers may stop visiting. Business owners may also spend money on additional security, repairs and relocation.
In some communities, business owners have been forced to close their shops after repeated attacks, threats or kidnappings. Even businesses that are not directly attacked can suffer when their customers, workers and suppliers become afraid to move around.
The 2024 State of Entrepreneurship in Nigeria report by FATE Foundation identified insecurity among the five major challenges facing entrepreneurs, alongside limited access to finance, poor electricity supply, foreign exchange difficulties and infrastructure challenges.
This finding is important because it shows that insecurity is not only a problem for people living in conflict-affected communities. It is also recognised by entrepreneurs as a major obstacle to doing business in Nigeria.
For a small business owner, spending money on security means having less money to invest in stock, equipment, staff or expansion.
Some businesses may survive by reducing their workforce or opening for fewer hours. Others may eventually close because their income can no longer cover their expenses. The result is a reduction in economic activities and fewer opportunities for people seeking employment.
Manufacturing and investment: Why businesses become cautious Nigeria’s manufacturing sector also depends on a stable business environment.
Manufacturers need access to raw materials, electricity, workers, transportation, customers and reliable markets. Insecurity can affect several of these needs at the same time.
When factories and warehouses are located in areas affected by violence, companies may face difficulties protecting their workers and properties. Insecurity can also disrupt the movement of raw materials and finished products, making production more expensive.
For investors, security is an important consideration before committing money to a new business.
An investor planning to establish a factory, warehouse, farm or distribution centre must consider whether workers can operate safely, whether goods can move without interruption and whether the business can remain open throughout the year.
When these conditions are uncertain, investors may delay their plans, reduce their investments or consider locations where business operations are safer.
The International Finance Corporation’s 2025 Nigeria Country Private Sector Diagnostic identified violent crime, kidnapping and conflict as concerns that undermine the country’s ability to attract private investment.
The report also highlighted other problems affecting businesses, including limited access to finance and foreign exchange challenges. This shows that insecurity is part of a wider business problem that requires attention.
Nigeria needs private investment to create jobs, improve production and expand its economy. But investors need confidence that their businesses, workers and investments will be protected.
The effect on food prices and the cost of living One of the most visible ways insecurity affects ordinary Nigerians is through food prices.
When farmers abandon their farms, food production can decline. When transporters avoid certain routes, the cost of moving agricultural products can increase. When markets are disrupted, the supply of goods can become unreliable.
These problems can contribute to higher food prices. The relationship between insecurity and food prices is not the only factor responsible for the rising cost of food in Nigeria. High fuel prices, the depreciation of the naira, expensive fertiliser, poor roads, storage problems and other economic challenges also play important roles.
However, insecurity makes an already difficult situation worse.
A family that previously spent a certain amount on food may discover that the same amount can no longer buy enough for the household. Restaurants, food vendors, bakeries and other businesses that depend on agricultural products also have to spend more on raw materials.
Some increase their prices, while others reduce the quantity of food they sell to customers. This creates a difficult situation for both business owners and consumers.
A business owner wants to remain profitable, but customers whose incomes have not increased may no longer be able to afford the new prices. Job losses and the growing number of people without regular income. Insecurity also affects employment because businesses cannot continue to employ workers when their operations are disrupted.
When a farm is abandoned, farm workers lose their source of income. When a market shuts down, traders and their assistants are affected. When a transport company reduces its operations, drivers, conductors, mechanics and other workers may suffer.
Small businesses are particularly vulnerable because they may not have enough money to continue paying salaries when sales decline.
The problem becomes more serious when displaced people move into safer communities in search of shelter and employment.
These movements can increase pressure on available jobs, housing, schools, healthcare facilities and other services.
For young Nigerians who are already struggling to find employment, the closure or relocation of businesses creates even fewer opportunities.
Insecurity therefore affects more than the people who are directly attacked. It also affects people who depend on businesses for their daily survival.
Oil and gas: Security challenges and national revenue Nigeria’s oil and gas industry is another important part of the economy that has faced security-related difficulties.
Oil theft, pipeline vandalism, illegal refining and attacks on oil infrastructure have affected production and created challenges for the country’s energy industry.
When pipelines and other oil facilities are attacked or damaged, companies may be forced to suspend operations while repairs are carried out.
These disruptions can affect crude oil production, government revenue and the earnings of businesses that provide services to the oil and gas industry. Companies operating in the sector also have to consider the cost of protecting their facilities, workers and equipment.
The effects can extend to oil-producing communities, where local businesses depend on spending by oil companies and their workers.
Although Nigeria’s oil production is influenced by several factors, including investment, maintenance, technical problems and production agreements, security breaches remain an important risk.
The Central Bank of Nigeria’s 2025 macroeconomic outlook also identified security breaches around oil installations as a possible threat to crude oil production and the country’s economic outlook for 2026.
The cost of insecurity is bigger than lost properties The economic damage caused by insecurity cannot be measured only by the value of buildings, vehicles, farms and shops destroyed during attacks.
There are other losses that are not always visible. A farmer who abandons his land loses the income he would have earned from the harvest. A trader who closes his shop loses daily sales. A transport company that stops operating on a particular route loses customers.
A manufacturer that cannot receive raw materials on time may lose production hours and business contracts. There is also the money businesses spend on security, insurance, relocation and alternative transportation arrangements.
The World Bank and other development institutions have repeatedly identified insecurity as a challenge to economic productivity and investment.
In its 2026 assessment of Nigeria, the International Monetary Fund also noted that insecurity continues to affect investment, agriculture and oil production.
These concerns show that the economic effects of insecurity are not temporary inconveniences. They can weaken the ability of businesses to grow, employ more people and contribute to national development.
What happens if the situation continues? If insecurity continues to affect farming communities, markets, transportation networks and business locations, Nigeria may face more difficulties in expanding local production.
Businesses may become more interested in protecting what they already have than investing in expansion.
Farmers may reduce the size of their cultivated land. Traders may limit the number of markets they visit. Transporters may avoid certain routes, while investors may delay projects.
Over time, these decisions can reduce economic activities, weaken supply chains and make goods more expensive.
The country also risks losing business opportunities to other economies that can offer investors a more stable operating environment.
For Nigeria, this is a serious concern because the country needs more productive businesses to create jobs, reduce poverty and improve the standard of living.
The way forward: Security must become an economic priority Addressing insecurity should not be treated only as a responsibility of the security agencies. It should also be seen as an important part of Nigeria’s economic development plans.
Farmers need to be able to visit their farms without fear of being kidnapped or attacked. Traders need safe access to markets, while transporters need secure roads to move people and goods.
The government must improve intelligence gathering, strengthen community-based security arrangements within the law and ensure that security agencies respond quickly to threats.
There should also be better protection for rural communities, particularly during planting and harvesting seasons.
For businesses, access to affordable insurance and financial support can help those affected by attacks to recover. Government agencies and business associations should also work together to identify areas where insecurity is disrupting commercial activities and develop practical solutions.
However, security operations alone may not solve the problem. Unemployment, poverty, weak local institutions and disputes over land and natural resources also require attention. Creating jobs, supporting rural businesses, improving infrastructure and strengthening justice systems are important parts of a lasting response.
Most importantly, people who commit kidnapping, attacks on farmers, destruction of property and other criminal activities must face the law.
An economy cannot grow where businesses are afraid Five years of insecurity have shown that violence does not affect only the communities where attacks take place. Its consequences travel through farms, markets, highways, factories and homes.
A farmer who cannot reach his farmland affects the food supply chain. A transporter who avoids a dangerous road affects the movement of goods. A trader who closes a shop affects customers, suppliers and workers. An investor who delays a project means fewer opportunities for employment and production.
These are the everyday economic consequences of insecurity that are sometimes overlooked when discussions focus only on the number of attacks and casualties.
Nigeria’s economic recovery requires more than policies aimed at controlling inflation, stabilising the naira or attracting investors. It also requires an environment where people can work, travel, farm and conduct business without living in constant fear.
Until farmers can safely return to their fields, traders can operate without fear, transporters can move goods freely and investors can protect their investments, the country’s business environment will continue to face serious challenges.
For millions of Nigerians whose livelihoods depend on daily business activities, security is not just about staying alive. It is also about being able to earn a living.
